title: What Is the Best Type of Attic Insulation?
h1: What Is the Best Type of Attic Insulation for Your Home?
description: Blown-in fiberglass, cellulose, batts, spray foam and radiant barriers each fit different attics. Compare the common types and see which suits your home.
quick_answer: For most existing attics, blown-in insulation, either fiberglass or cellulose, is the best fit because it fills gaps and covers irregular spaces well. Batts work in open, standard-spaced attics. Spray foam suits special cases like sealing an unvented attic. The best choice depends on your attic layout, budget and existing insulation.
body:
There isn't one best insulation for every attic. The right choice depends on the shape of the space, what's already there, whether there are rodent or moisture issues, and what you want to achieve. Here's how the common types compare in a typical Southern California home.

What are the main types of attic insulation?

Blown-in fiberglass

Loose fiberglass is blown across the attic floor with a machine. It fills around wiring, framing and obstacles, and it can be added on top of existing clean insulation. Fiberglass doesn't absorb much water and doesn't provide food for pests, though rodents can still nest in it. It's one of the most common choices for existing homes.

Blown-in cellulose

Cellulose is made mostly from recycled paper treated with fire retardants. It's denser than loose fiberglass, which helps it resist air movement through the insulation layer. It can settle more over time and doesn't handle getting wet as well, so roof leaks need to be fixed first.

Fiberglass or mineral wool batts

Batts come in pre-cut blankets sized to fit between joists. They work well in open attics with standard joist spacing and few obstacles. They're less effective when cut poorly or squeezed around wiring and pipes, because gaps and compression reduce performance. Mineral wool batts handle heat and moisture well and are more fire resistant than fiberglass.

Spray foam

Spray foam is applied as a liquid that expands and hardens. Open-cell and closed-cell foam both seal air leaks well. It's often used on the underside of the roof deck to create an unvented, conditioned attic, which can make sense when ducts and HVAC equipment are in the attic. It costs more, requires careful installation and makes future roof or wiring work harder.

Radiant barriers

A radiant barrier is a reflective foil layer installed under the roof deck or over the rafters. It reflects radiant heat from the roof and can help keep attics cooler in hot climates. It's not a substitute for insulation on the attic floor but can work alongside it, especially in inland homes with strong summer sun.

How do they compare?

TypeBest forThings to know

Blown-in celluloseExisting attics, better air resistanceCan settle, keep it dry
BattsOpen attics with standard joist spacingMust be cut and fit carefully

Which is best for a typical San Diego attic?

Many homes in the area have low-pitched attics with ducts, a furnace and wiring running through them. Blown-in insulation fills around all of that without much cutting and fitting. In homes where the existing insulation is clean, new blown-in insulation can go right on top. If rodents or water have damaged the old insulation, it should be removed first.

Inland homes with hot afternoon sun may also benefit from a radiant barrier. Coastal homes with milder temperatures usually get the most value from proper depth and good air sealing.

Does air sealing matter as much as the insulation type?

Often more. Air leaks around light fixtures, wiring holes, plumbing vents, top plates and the attic hatch let air move freely between the house and attic. Fiberglass and cellulose don't stop that air movement on their own. Sealing those gaps before insulating makes any type perform better.

How do you choose?

  1. Look at what's in the attic now and whether it's clean and dry.
  2. Consider the layout: obstacles, joist spacing and headroom.
  3. Decide whether you want to keep a vented attic or create an unvented one.
  4. Factor in your budget and how long you plan to stay in the home.
  5. Get an inspection that includes air leaks, ventilation and ducts.

faqs: Is blown-in or batt insulation better for an attic?
For most existing attics, blown-in insulation is the better fit because it fills around wiring, ducts and framing without gaps. Batts can work well in open attics with standard joist spacing.
Both work well. Cellulose is denser and resists air movement better, while fiberglass handles moisture better and settles less. The right choice depends on your attic and existing insulation.
Is spray foam worth it in an attic?

It can be when you want an unvented, conditioned attic, such as when ducts and HVAC equipment are up there. It costs more and needs careful professional installation, so it is not the default choice for most homes.
Do radiant barriers work in Southern California?
They can help keep attics cooler in hot, sunny inland areas. They work alongside insulation on the attic floor rather than replacing it.
What Insulation Is Most Mold Resistant?

Mineral wool and closed-cell spray foam are among the most mold-resistant insulation types, and fiberglass and rigid foam boards don't feed mold on their own. Cellulose is treated to resist mold but can hold water if it gets wet. No insulation is mold-proof, though. Dust and moisture can still grow mold on almost any surface.
